standfirst: A teenage shaman hides her work from her classmates and quietly starts spending her luck to keep the unluckiest boy in school alive. For eight episodes it is the best young romance of 2025, with rules simple enough to care about and a best friend who knows he is losing. Then a new character arrives around episode nine and the ending belongs to a different story. These picks are the fated love and supernatural romances that hold their shape to the last hour.

picks.why: The same premise, executed all the way through. Somebody sees what is coming, tries to prevent it, and pays a price for interfering. Same tension between a gift and a normal life, same central question of what you owe a person you can save. Difference: the leads are adults in a legal procedural, so the plotting is tighter and the school romance sweetness is gone.

For the youth fantasy that earns its emotion. A teenager pulled into a situation with rules he did not choose, music as the emotional engine, and a family knot underneath the high school surface. Difference: it is about parents rather than fate, and it does not lose its way in the back half, which is the one thing Head Over Heels cannot claim.

If the shamanism was the draw: possession, spirits, and a heroine whose gift makes her an outsider in her own household. Same world logic, sixteen episodes of it. Difference: Joseon setting, an adult romance, and a much lighter tone. The mortal danger that gives this show its urgency is largely decorative there.

Supernatural rules, a mortal caught in them, and a romance that has to survive a mythology. Same structure of a gifted protector and someone who keeps needing protecting. Difference: contemporary, adult, and considerably more violent, with the immortal doing the saving rather than a schoolgirl spending her own luck.

For the doomed romance with an afterlife rulebook. Ghosts with unfinished business, a lead who cannot be saved by loving someone, and production design carrying half the mood. Difference: it is a glossy melodrama about a very long grudge, so it trades the school setting and the first love ache for spectacle and sadness.

The other recent show where seeing the dead is a job rather than a gift. Case of the week structure, workplace comedy, and a lead who would rather not have the ability. Difference: no romance and no fate. It is a labour law procedural with ghosts, aimed at anger about workplaces instead of teenage longing.

against.title: Lovely Runner
against.why: The default pick for saving the person you love from dying, and the resemblance is close enough to be dangerous. That show has a clean deadline, keeps its rules honest and lands its ending. This one abandons its premise in the last third. Watch Lovely Runner second and Head Over Heels will look worse in retrospect.

against.title: Goblin
against.why: Paired for fated love with a supernatural cost, and it is a much bigger, slower thing. The buildup runs to episode eight and the register is mythic rather than teenage. If the school corridor romance is what you wanted, Goblin will feel like homework.

against.title: The Uncanny Counter
against.why: Suggested because it is the other show where a young person fights the supernatural. It is a team based action series with a demon hunting hierarchy and no interest in romance. The ache that drives Head Over Heels is absent by design.
